chapter: Chicago cafes and the Browns band
title: Wadsworth, Bert Kelly and the College Inn dance band job
summary: Wadsworth landed the College Inn job in 1915 despite Blaufus blocking union entry; Bert Kelly became the front man paid by the boss, and the band later broke up.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: The Browns band, well, I tell you, they eventually split up. Uh, Waddy Wasworth, who was in that, uh, College Inn band, it was Waddy that landed that job at the College Inn in 1915, February. They had never had dancing at the College Inn before. Strictly an orchestra, straight legit orchestra that, in between skating shows, they just sat there and played a concert, a semi-concert number once in a while.
It was in the basement. In the College Inn.

In the College Inn. And they had an ice skating rink there for the performers. So, Walter Blaufus had the orchestra down there for the skating show and everything. And when he heard that they were going to put in a dance band, he went to the union and kept them from coming in. He kept them from, uh, so that they couldn't join the union. He fixed it up. Oh, yeah, I see. I see. So, uh, the Sherman House said, okay, you can get out and they can, they'll come in anyhow. Well, when Walter was about to lose the job down there and they were going to cut out the ice skating show, then Walter, after trying, like, all get out to keep them from joining the union, he went over there and fought with his fingernails almost, I guess, to, to get them into the union. And he, they got into the union and they went down there and started to play for dancing. And they alternated between the skating shows and dancing.

Waddy Wadsworth landed the job, the saxophone player, who had had the band at the Winter Garden that I told you about. And, uh, so, Bert Kelly was a pretty smart guy. And he, he said to the boys as they were getting there at the end of the week, he said, gee, he says, uh, here are the four of us. We are here. We got the job. We ought to have somebody that could talk to the boss. And Bert says, I'll talk to him. He, he's the one that brought it up. And he also said, I'll talk to him. If that's all right. They said, okay. So he not only talked to the boss, but when it was time for them to get paid, they got paychecks signed by Bert Kelly.
You mean the boss would pay Bert and then Bert split it up?
That's right. It was Bert Kelly's job. He finagled and it was his job.
Well, Bert had gotten in with, uh, Wadsworth then.

Wadsworth was the guy that, uh, really booked the job and landed the job and hired Kelly as the banjo player. So from then on, uh, uh, Kelly, and it was, I guess it was Erking Wadsworth pretty much. And they, if Wadsworth probably was out of there and that's when Kelly got Gus Miller to come in to play clarinet and tenor saxophone. And he, uh, Gus. And the band had broken up. And that's what broke up the band. Uh, Ray Lopez, uh, went with another band over at the, uh, Windcliff Inn. I told you about that too, I think. It was in the basement of the Windsor Clifton Hotel where, that's where Carson Perry's Cotton Company's men's store is now. And Benny Fields and Benny Davis and Jack Salisbury were a singing trio in the Windcliff Inn. And, uh, Ray Lopez was, uh, in the band. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
